newsitem.title: VIETNAM: U.S. journalist compelled to leave Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: U.S. journalist compelled to leave Vietnam.

text.p: Vietnam said on Thursday it had refused to renew a visa for an American correspondent in Hanoi, prompting a veiled warning from a U.S. diplomat over the impact of the move on international sentiment towards Vietnam.
A short statement issued by the Foreign Ministry said the authorities would not renew a visa for journalist Adam Schwarz, 35, of the Far Eastern Economic Review magazine.
"We find it impossible to extend it. It's a normal thing," the statement said, adding:

"We'd like to take this opportunity to reconfirm that Vietnam's policy is always to welcome and create favourable conditions for foreign correspondents to come and carry out press activities in Vietnam within the Vietnamese legal framework and current regulations and with goodwill towards contributing to mutual understanding between nations."
An American diplomat issued a counter-statement later praising Schwarz's work and hinting that Hanoi's decision might prejudice foreign views of Vietnam.
"He provided an important service by informing investors and potential investors of risks and opportunities in Vietnam," the statement said.
"It reassured them that correspondents like Mr Schwarz were working here. It was seen as evidence that Vietnam is serious about economic reforms and openness."
Vietnam opened its doors to foreign correspondents in the late 1980s.

Since then a number of international news organisations have set up bureaux in the capital, Hanoi, to report on a country changing from an orthodox socialist system to a capitalist-style market economy.
But relations between the communist government and the foreign media have remained delicate.
Hanoi has been sensitive to reports indicating problems in its investment environment and has accused foreign news organisations in recent months of failing to understand its socialist system.
Reporting of political issues, such as details of the inner workings of the Communist Party, is considered similarly touchy.
But the decision to refuse Schwarz a visa marks the first time a resident correspondent has been formally compelled to leave since reform policies were launched in 1986.
Far Eastern Economic Review editor Joseph Kahn said on Thursday he was disappointed by the decision.
"We are happy with Adam's coverage," he said by phone from Hong Kong. "But the Vietnamese had another impression, and it's clearly their country."
Kahn added that the Review, a Hong Kong-based subsidiary of U.S. firm Dow Jones and Company Inc, was planning to post another correspondent to Hanoi in the near future.
Schwarz began his assignment in Vietnam in 1994. The Review opened its Hanoi office in 1990.
